dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: ahaṃ mamedam ityādi pratipattiprasaṅgataḥ | nirādhāre mano yāti taddhyānapreraṇāc chamī ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
dharana.rendering: On the occasion of thoughts like 'I am', 'this is mine', the mind goes to what has no support; impelled by contemplating that, one becomes peaceful.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the supportless is the absolute 'I' (pūrṇāham), free of thought-constructs, present behind the everyday 'I' in the ignorant and the wise alike; whenever one says 'I', the mind subconsciously reflects it, and contemplating that thought-free 'I' as one's real Self, a pure thought ends in thought-free awareness (citing Tantrāloka 1.214–215). He classes it as śāktopāya. Wallis: when you hear yourself say 'I am…' or 'this is mine', inquire what 'I' or 'my' refers to; the mind looks for a referent and cannot find one.
dharana.technique_name: 'I' and 'Mine': Following Them to No Support
dharana.instruction: When you think 'I' or 'mine', ask what it refers to, and rest in the open awareness you find.

checked_against: The Mystery Within (2019), Session Two list: 'Dharana 106' = verse 131 (agrees with Singh)

verification.notes: Door index = Singh dhāraṇā number, read directly in Singh's own headings and cross-checked against The Mystery Within's Singh-numbered list and Wallis's concordance. Caveat: Singh was read from an OCR scan, not a print copy in hand.

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 131: No self, no basis, no support needed (Y106 ~ B2)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 131 'Dharana 108', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 106. Not followed.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 131 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the thought 'I' or 'mine' traced back to where it comes from, and finding no solid support there.
geometry.svg_hint: an arrow labelled 'I' tracing back to an open, unsupported space
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Trace 'I' back
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: each 'I' and 'mine' is traced back and found to rest on nothing solid, only open awareness. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: wherever the breath naturally ends; this door places nothing on the breath
breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Turn attention toward what the verse names, and let everything else stay in the background
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.primary: The everyday thoughts 'I' and 'mine', as they occur
attention.secondary: The supportless awareness they point back to

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: On the occasion of thoughts like 'I am', 'this is mine', the mind goes to what has no support; impelled by contemplating that, one becomes peaceful.
adiyogi.method_summary: When you notice yourself thinking or saying 'I am…' or 'this is mine', pause. Ask what the 'I' refers to. Let the mind look, and when it finds nothing solid, rest in that open, supportless awareness.

honesty.disclosure: Door 106 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 106 (verse 131) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. Ownership and responsibility in daily life still matter; this is an inner inquiry, not a rule for practical affairs. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
